question: Fans of this Japanese remix tradition use soramimi, hearing English dialogue as unrelated Japanese phrases and adding humorous subtitles. Its best-known performer visited Japan in 2009, when a figma action figure modeled on him was announced to enthusiastic fans. Billy Herrington became a central figure in this community, whose fans affectionately addressed him as “Aniki”, meaning an older brother. For 10 points, name this Nico Nico meme tradition that turns footage of muscular men wrestling into elaborate musical mashups and remixed videos.

This song debuted through a three-member unit brought together by the Love Live franchise’s All Night Nippon Gold radio program. Its performers include Aguri Onishi and Wakana Okuma, whose characters Ayumu and Shiki come from different school-idol groups. A clip posted by the franchise’s official TikTok account spread a call-and-response segment from a February 2025 live performance. In that segment, each performer names an ice-cream flavor before declaring that the listener is an even greater favorite. For 10 points, name this viral idol song or trend in which a high-pitched voice enthusiastically professes affection beyond chocolate mint.
answer: Ai Scream! [or Ai♡Scream!; or Ruby-chan Hai; or Ruby-chan; or Ai Sukurīmu; or Ai Sukurimu]

question: This song shared a physical single release with “Nidone”, another track by the same duo, in March 2024. Its production uses a Jersey club rhythm, bringing that dance-music style into a Japanese rap performance released earlier that year. The opening animation accompanying this track inspired a dance challenge built around movements performed by its anime’s muscular protagonist. Creepy Nuts supplied this theme for the Divine Visionary Candidate Exam arc, the second season of its associated series. For 10 points, name this rapidly chanted opening song from Mashle, whose hero compensates for lacking magic through physical strength.

This song’s creator explained that its chorus began as the English phrase “get it get it done” before being rewritten phonetically. Illustrator Kazuya Kanehisa supplied its animated video, using a retro style recalling manga and cartoons from the Showa era. Its creator described the track as an SOS, expressing the need for help beneath its energetic musical presentation. Released in May 2024, it gained overseas listeners and received an English-language version at the end of July. For 10 points, name this Kocchi no Kento hit, or the viral choreography associated with its repeated, urgently delivered chorus.

Tetsuji Hayashi composed this song’s music and Yoshiko Miura wrote its lyrics; it later appeared on the album Pocket Park. The original performer recorded this debut single at nineteen, releasing it in 1979 before its much later international rediscovery. Indonesian singer Rainych helped revive this track through a 2020 cover, decades after its original release in Japan. Another route into its revival involved TikTok users playing the recording for their Japanese mothers and filming their recognition. For 10 points, name this Miki Matsubara city-pop song, whose English refrain pleads for a lover’s continued presence.
answer: Stay With Me [or Mayonaka no Door; or Mayonaka no Doa; or Mayonaka no Door Stay with Me]

question: A version of this dish associated with the film Tampopo was developed through a collaboration involving the Tokyo restaurant Taimeiken. It belongs to yoshoku, the Japanese tradition of adapting Western food, and its name combines French and English food words. A familiar home-style preparation encloses its filling in a thin egg layer, while other versions use a softer topping. That filling commonly includes fried rice, chicken and ketchup, although a demi-glace sauce can also accompany the finished plate. For 10 points, name this Japanese omelette-and-rice dish, often featured in videos where a knife opens the soft egg covering.

The official video for this track arrived in 2023, although the song itself had already been released three years earlier. Its creators chose locations suggesting the Showa era for that video, giving the already popular track an appropriately retro visual setting. This song received the grand prize at the TikTok awards covering trends from the first half of 2023. The four members of Atarashii Gakko supplied the performance that brought its chorus choreography to a much wider audience. For 10 points, name this Atarashii Gakko hit associated with the distinctive side-to-side neck movements copied in a viral dance.

Satoru Kosaki composed this song with lyrics by Meg Rock, and its recording accompanied the fourth home-video volume of its anime. Kana Hanazawa performs the track in character as Nadeko Sengoku, whose story provides the context for its original appearance. The song serves as the opening for episode ten of Bakemonogatari, during the arc involving that character and a snake curse. Fan covers and mashups circulated on Nico Nico Douga before the song reached international TikTok audiences, including through an English-language version. For 10 points, name this cute, softly rapped Nadeko opening theme that became a widely reused anime song online.

Alstroemeria Records placed a vocal arrangement of this tune on Lovelight, with nomico singing and Masayoshi Minoshima supplying the remix. Its source melody was composed by ZUN for the third stage of Lotus Land Story, a game released in 1998. A 2009 fan animation credited to Anira paired the vocal version with figures from the Touhou series changing into one another. Fans have recreated that animation using unusual displays, including Minecraft sheep and the collaborative pixel canvas known as r/place. For 10 points, name this Touhou song best recognized through its music video of animated silhouettes rendered entirely in black and white.

The music added to this clip comes from John Morris’s score for Young Frankenstein, a comedy released in 1974. Its animal footage originally appeared in a segment featuring the idol group MiniMoni and a transparent enclosure on Japanese morning television. The edited excerpt spread across sites including YouTube in 2007, turning a brief piece of Japanese television into an international meme. The rodent suddenly swivels toward the camera, which then zooms closer as a suspenseful musical sting emphasizes its apparent alarm. For 10 points, name this five-second reaction video, commonly named for a different small rodent than the one actually shown.

The Laziest Men on Mars incorporated this phrase into “Invasion of the Gabber Robots”, a techno track built around video-game music. Bad_CRC paired that recording with an animated music video posted on Newgrounds in February 2001, helping spread the phrase widely. Its original English wording came from a Toaplan employee handling overseas business rather than a professional translator working on the script. The villain CATS delivers this announcement during the introductory sequence of the 1991 European Mega Drive version of Zero Wing. For 10 points, give this famously ungrammatical declaration that the enemy has captured every military installation previously controlled by the player’s side.
answer: All Your Base Are Belong to Us [or All Your Base; or AYBABTU]

question: This animation loops a scat-singing passage from a Finnish recording included on the 1995 album Things of Beauty. The image uses four frames taken from the second episode of Bleach, where a character discusses food with Ichigo and Rukia. The original Flash animation combined those frames with a short audio loop and spread around the internet in 2006. A scat-singing excerpt from “Ievan Polkka” accompanies the animation, matching its nonsensical syllables to the repeated movement of a bunching onion. For 10 points, name this looping meme showing Orihime Inoue cheerfully twirling a green vegetable in her hand.

The animation associated with this meme borrows movements from Mai and Mii in the opening sequence of the game Popotan. A sped-up version attributed to Speedycake helped transform the original recording into the soundtrack used by many later fan animations. That original track appeared on Supergott, a 2001 album by the Swedish group Caramell, before its international online popularity. The dance spread through Japanese video culture, with participants swinging their hips while holding their hands beside their heads. For 10 points, name this Swedish-language song and anime dance meme recognizable by its raised hands imitating rabbit ears.

This track appeared on Super Eurobeat Presents Euromach 2 in 1999, before becoming especially closely associated with a racing anime. The recording was used in episode thirteen of Initial D Second Stage, then included on a compilation devoted to that series. Online Eurobeat remix compilations reused the song, helping turn its association with anime racing into a recognizable internet audio joke. Dave Rodgers performs this track, whose French title describes the sensation that a present experience has somehow happened before. For 10 points, name this Initial D song with a two-word title meaning “already seen”, familiar from racing-themed meme videos.

An early version of this meme showed the elongated character 8toushin swaying his hips over an instrumental by Gojimaji-P. Riotto-P made an influential colored version of its head-bobbing character animation, providing another template for video creators to imitate. Gojimaji-P, also known as Lamaze-P, created both the original 2010 animation and another showing Kasane Teto’s moving head. Fans replaced the character or made their own vocal performances, including a popular cover recorded by the singer Lon. For 10 points, name this rapidly bobbing-head meme associated with Kasane Teto, or the mischievous-sounding song commonly used with it.

This single paired its main track with the B-side “Welcome Unknown”, with lyrics supplied by Aki Hata and music by Tomokazu Tashiro. Yutaka Yamamoto directed its ending animation, whose choreography incorporates movements resembling routines performed by the idol group Berryz Kobo. Aya Hirano, Minori Chihara and Yuko Goto sing the track as their characters from a 2006 school-club anime. The sequence accompanying the song’s end credits became widely imitated, with fans performing its synchronized movements outside the original animation. For 10 points, name this cheerful ending theme whose routine features the SOS Brigade, including Yuki Nagato and Mikuru Asahina.

This meme grew from a Japanese advertising campaign that answered questions about a mascot, directing viewers online for the explanations. An early edit spliced the commercials together with footage from Ultraman Mebius, before a Touhou mashup reached audiences overseas. That later edit matched the clown’s movements and vocal sounds to “U.N. Owen Was Her”, creating a frantic musical montage. In the original commercials, the mascot describes a three-syllable chant and accompanying gestures as something he does when feeling happy. For 10 points, name this repeated chant or remix meme featuring the hamburger-selling clown associated with the Golden Arches.
answer: Ran Ran Ru [or Ronald McDonald Insanity; or McRoll; or Ran Ran Ruu]

question: An animated version of this meme makes the elongated 8toushin Mona character gyrate frantically to a Japanese pop chorus. The name of this meme comes from listeners’ rendering of an English phrase heard just before a Japanese song’s chorus. A 2007 Nico Nico video showed a Nintendo 64 game running with its cartridge only partly inserted, producing wildly rotating figures. An edit paired that footage with Kohmi Hirose’s 1997 song “promise”, connecting its chorus with the characters’ erratic movement. For 10 points, name this spinning dance meme rooted in a GoldenEye 007 cartridge glitch and a Japanese pop chorus.

This song received a jazz arrangement by the Baguettes Ensemble and appeared in the medley Nanairo no Nico Nico Douga. Its creator later made versions featuring Kasane Teto, Megurine Luka and Kagamine Rin, as well as an English-language performance. Lamaze-P supplied the music, lyrics and illustration for the original Hatsune Miku recording, uploaded during December 2008 on Nico Nico. The singer enthusiastically recommends a green drink in this track, treating it as something the listener should come to love. For 10 points, name this bouncy Vocaloid song in which Miku promotes a healthy beverage with a price of 200 yen.

This man reached the Wimbledon quarterfinals in 1995, years before his unusually intense encouragement became material for online musical remixes. After his tennis career, he appeared as a television commentator on both sporting events and programs involving food. His website’s “For You” videos offered motivational messages, and Nico Nico users turned clips of his energetic delivery into MAD edits. In an especially recognizable clip, he encourages perseverance while standing in cold water and explaining that he is gathering clams. For 10 points, name this Japanese former tennis player whose emphatic English demand to keep trying became an international encouragement meme.

Fans imagined this animal fighting a dark rival named Tacgnol in a fictional apocalyptic conflict they called Catnarok. Its stretched appearance was later compared with the Gigantamax form of Meowth introduced in the Pokémon Sword and Shield games. The original photograph became popular through Japan’s Futaba Channel, then circulated internationally as a template for increasingly exaggerated image edits. This white feline was photographed being held beneath its front legs, leaving its body dangling vertically toward the ground. For 10 points, name this internet-famous Japanese pet whose meme emphasizes the remarkable apparent length of its torso.

Sebastian Masuda, associated with the fashion brand 6%DOKIDOKI, supplied the art direction for this song’s colorful and surreal music video. Director Jun Tamukai filled that video with strange visual moments, including a microphone emerging from the performer’s ear. The song was written and produced by Yasutaka Nakata, and appeared on the EP Moshi Moshi Harajuku in 2011. One gag makes bread appear when the performer claps, playing on the Japanese word for that food and the sound of clapping. For 10 points, name this Kyary Pamyu Pamyu debut single whose repeated-syllable title accompanied an internationally viral explosion of kawaii imagery.

The audio behind this meme appeared on an Astral Trip album released at Comiket 76, before its better-known animated video circulated. That recording remixes a Touhou composition called “Broken Moon”, tying the later internet joke to the game series’ fan-music scene. A 2010 video paired the music with a three-dimensional model of Suika Ibuki performing an energetic routine against a simple background. A subtitled YouTube upload helped carry the animation beyond Nico Nico, and another wave of edits appeared in 2022. For 10 points, name this meme whose English refrain identifies the dancing Touhou character using a nationality followed by a folkloric creature.

This remix appeared on the album Hanataba, released for the 2007 Reitaisai event devoted to a bullet-hell game series. Its arranger, BeatMARIO, belongs to COOL&CREATE and reworked a theme associated with Sakuya Izayoi into a much faster track. Its source melody accompanies Sakuya Izayoi in the ninth main Touhou game, linking this track to the series’ fan-music tradition. Nico Nico users made numerous remixes and performances using this energetic arrangement, which became popular there during 2008. For 10 points, name this fast Touhou remix whose English title repeats a word for the hours after sunset.

A longer version of this track appeared on Tatsh’s album Material, while its arcade form was labeled with the genre “SPEED RAVE”. Its performance credits combine Tatsh’s composition and arrangement with guitar played by NAOKI, while Kraig E supplies the vocals. The song first appeared in Konami’s eleventh beatmania IIDX release, becoming one of the signature tracks associated with that edition. A 2009 fan edit helped popularize a split-screen presentation that later makers of musical MAD videos repeatedly adapted. For 10 points, name this Tatsh and NAOKI rhythm-game track whose two-word English title describes a scarlet-colored area.

Taro made this song using GarageBand, creating a recording whose spoken exchanges supplied material for numerous later animated interpretations. The song was released in 2006, then reached Nico Nico users through a 2007 upload before a wave of subsequent parodies. Its dialogue concerns a teacher and a class representative organizing students during a trip, with their arrangement becoming a rhythmic dispute. Fans turned the recording into both character animations and live-action dance performances, expanding the joke beyond its original musical release. For 10 points, name this Japanese meme song whose short title combines the words for males and females, repeatedly chanted in alternation.
